question: Q81
summary: Francophone historians did engage Who Killed Canadian History? (1998), but only as reviewers, in French-language venues and the CHA Bulletin. There were at least six responses in 1998-99: Dionne (RHAF 1998); Bouvier, Fahmy-Eid, Jedwab and Slogar, and Dubuc (BHP 1999); Dumont (CHA Bulletin 1999). No francophone reply to Bliss (1991-92) was found; the JCS respondents were all anglophone. Quebec ran its own debate on its own terms. It began with the BHP's calls for political history (1992, 1995) and Bélanger's 'Pour un retour à l'histoire politique' (RHAF 1997). Comeau and Dionne's volume followed (1998), then the 2006-07 curriculum controversy, Petitclerc's defence of social history (2009) and Bédard and D'Arcy's 'L'histoire nationale négligée' (2011). Its checked texts do not cite the English-Canadian debate, and English Canada appears in them only as a foil (multiculturalism, Historica). The engagement ran one way and through a few bridge figures: Dionne, Bouvier, Dumont and Létourneau. Anglophones met the Quebec side only through Létourneau's 2000 CHR forum.

q1_direct_francophone_responses.to_bliss_1991: None found. The JCS 1992 replies are all anglophone (G. Kealey; L. Kealey, Pierson, Sangster, Strong-Boag; Fleming; Comacchio). The BHP 1997 editorial 'Vers une privatisation de l'histoire?' is a false lead: it concerns judicial records.
q1_direct_francophone_responses.chr_forum_2000: Létourneau's essay answers the debate's question (one unitarist narrative or fragmentation) and proposes 'canadianité'. The abstract does not name Granatstein or Bliss. The respondents were all anglophone. Tillotson (2019) cites the forum next to McKillop's Who Killed reply.
q1_direct_francophone_responses.fecteau_1999: About Rudin and Quebec revisionism, not Who Killed. It is the wrong evidence for a francophone voice in this debate.
q1_direct_francophone_responses.uptake: None of the francophone reviews is cited by any PhD in the graph. Granatstein 1998 is cited by 17 strict PhDs, 2 of them francophone.

phases: 1992-97: the BHP (first issue 1992) campaigns for political history: Bellavance 1992, Sarra-Bournet 1995, Bélanger 1997 (RHAF). Bélanger blames Annales and social history and does not refer to Bliss.

1998-2000: national history and school history: Comeau and Dionne, eds., 1998 (with Ferretti on the US national standards); Bouchard, 'Le social et l'actuel: deux clés pour la réécriture de l'histoire nationale' (BHP 7:3, 1999; title only); Létourneau 2000.
2006-07: the controversy over the Histoire et éducation à la citoyenneté programme (Le Devoir, 27 April 2006; Dagenais and Laville 2007; Bouvier 2008).
2007-12: the identity and neglect phase: Bock-Côté 2007; Petitclerc 2009 (social history's reply); Bédard and D'Arcy 2011; Bédard 2011; Bouvier et al. 2012.
q2_parallel_quebec_debate.structural_parallel: Same structure (political or national historians charge social history with fragmenting or denationalizing; social historians reply), but the nation is a different one: the Quebec debate defends a Quebec national narrative and treats Canadian multiculturalism and Canadian nation-building (Historica) as part of the problem.
q2_parallel_quebec_debate.engagement_with_english_debate: No checked Quebec-debate text cites Bliss or Granatstein: Bélanger 1997 (reprint check); Bouvier 2008 (full text searched); abstracts of Dagenais and Laville 2007 and Petitclerc 2009. The links run through people (Dionne, Bouvier, Dumont, Létourneau), not through texts.

recommendation.rationale: The user asked whether francophones engaged. They did, directly, with Granatstein in 1998-99, so the debate entry should show it. The Quebec debate is a related but separate quarrel, and the texts show no exchange between the two debates. A parallel strand or a merged francophone entry would overstate their connection, and most of the Quebec debate falls after 2000, outside the entry's coverage. The comparison edge already drafted (cdng_wk_rel_07 to quebec_historiography) should stay as drafted, with its evidence re-grounded: replace Fecteau 1999 (Rudin) with Dumont 1999, who ties Who Killed to Comeau and Dionne 1998 and to Létourneau.
concrete_changes_proposed: Add Micheline Dumont (already on the quebec_historiography and cdn_women_gender rosters) as a who_killed_debate critic, sourced to the full text of her 1999 CHA Bulletin review.

Add Bernard Dionne (RHAF 1998) and Nadia Fahmy-Eid (BHP 1999) as title-level critics, with review_status needs_review because their texts are unread. Félix Bouvier, Jack Jedwab and Grégory Slogar, and Alfred Dubuc can be cited in the description or sources without roster rows. Dubuc's first page is checked: he frames the book as mourning both national history and 'l'histoire politique comme discipline'.

Change the scope note's 'largely English-Canadian': the exchange was English-Canadian, but francophone historians answered Granatstein in RHAF, the BHP and the CHA Bulletin. They read the book as a lament for political and pan-Canadian unity history and corrected its claims about Quebec schooling. Quebec's own decline-of-national-history debate (BHP from 1992; Bélanger 1997; 2006-07 programme; Bédard and D'Arcy 2011) ran separately.
Keep Létourneau 2000. Move Fecteau 1999 from who_killed_debate to quebec_historiography only (the Rudin debate).
Later, not now: the post-2000 Quebec debate (2006-2012) could become its own Debate entry if coverage is ever extended past 2000. 19 strict PhDs cite its core texts, 12 of them francophone.

sources.citation: Alfred Dubuc, 'À propos de : Qui a tué l'histoire du Canada ?', Bulletin d'histoire politique 8, no. 1 (1999): 195ff.
sources.content: OpenAlex first-page excerpt read: Granatstein mourns the death of national history 'en particulier, et, plus généralement, celui de l'histoire politique comme discipline; par un effet domino, ce double crime fait d'autres victimes: la fierté nationale, le patriotisme, l'unité canadienne'; lists the eight culprits of Granatstein's last chapter (provincial ministries, their officials, ethnic communities and multiculturalism, school boards, media, university professors...). Search-engine summary gives the end page as 209 (not_verified). Dubuc's own verdict not read.
sources.role: Essay-length francophone response; frames Who Killed as also a lament for political history, the BHP's own cause.

sources.citation: Micheline Dumont, 'J.L. Granatstein, Who Killed Canadian History? Harper Collins, 1998: un compte-rendu', Canadian Historical Association Bulletin 25, no. 1 (1999): 12-14.
checked: PDF text layer (3 pages) read in full
sources.content: Read in full. Organized around the four words of the title. Points: Granatstein's information on Quebec schooling is 'erronée'; the 'killers' are 'les acteurs d'une conjoncture inédite', not assassins; history is not dead but 'a envahi tous les milieux'; what died is 'une certaine conception de l'histoire canadienne ... devenue caduque'; his 'réquisitoire est féroce contre les praticiens de l'histoire sociale'; the 1950s historians judged a single Canadian history textbook impossible 'dans les deux communautés nationales'; 'repousse du revers de la main toute vision de l'histoire canadienne qui ne vise pas l'unité canadienne. On ne trahit pas plus clairement des visées politiques'; criticizes the military-history emphasis from a gender perspective. She cites Lucia Ferretti's chapter in Comeau and Dionne, eds., À propos de l'histoire nationale (1998), 65-76, and Jocelyn Létourneau's surveys of students. Says the book's shadow hung over McGill Institute for the Study of Canada's colloquium 'Giving the Past a Future / L'Avenir de notre passé' (January 1999), where many social historians introduced themselves as 'killer of canadian history'. Year 1999 inferred from vol. 25 and the 'récent colloque' of January 1999; repository date 2020 is the deposit date.
sources.role: Strongest checked francophone voice; explicitly joins Who Killed to the Quebec national-history debate (Comeau-Dionne, Létourneau). Micheline Dumont is already on the quebec_historiography and cdn_women_gender rosters.

sources.citation: Jocelyn Létourneau, 'L'avenir du Canada: par rapport à quelle histoire?', CHR 81, no. 2 (2000): 229ff.; Forum (230-301) with Cook, Valverde, Miller, Owram, Tillotson, Palmer, Iacovetta, Mitchinson.
sources.content: Abstract: doubts an all-encompassing metanarrative; Canada needs neither a 'unitariste' nor an 'atomisant' narrative but a level of historiographic articulation that represents Canada 'dans ses maillages dissonants'; proposes 'canadianité'. The abstract does not name Granatstein or Bliss; whether the text does is not_verified (UTP paywall). All eight forum respondents are anglophone. Tillotson's centenary essay (CHR 100:3, 2019, doi:10.3138/chr.2018-0104; deposited notes fn52-53) cites McKillop's Who Killed reply and then Létourneau's forum together, which suggests the CHR placed the forum in the post-Granatstein moment (note placement only; text unread).
sources.role: Francophone intervention addressed to anglophones; answers the debate's question (one national narrative or fragments) rather than Granatstein by name.

sources.content: Abstract: analyses Rudin's Making History in Twentieth-Century Quebec, the role of nationhood in the 'revisionist school', and Rudin's epistemology. No reference to Bliss or Granatstein in the abstract.

sources.content: Abstract: diagnoses of 'crise' in Quebec social history in the 1990s gave way around 2000 to a radical critique rejecting social history as a modernist narrative contemptuous of tradition, championing a new history of ideas; calls for a 'refondation' of critical social history. Issue year 2009 from the graph; Crossref's only date is the 2010 online date.

sources.citation: Michèle Dagenais and Christian Laville, 'Le naufrage du projet de programme d'histoire « nationale »', RHAF 60, no. 4 (2007): 517-50.
sources.content: Abstract: 'Au coeur de 2006, une vive polémique a éclaté' over the reform of the secondary national-history programme; examines its stakes, actors, the relation between historical and citizenship education, and whether the polemic was scientifically justified.
sources.role: 2006-07 curriculum controversy.

sources.citation: Félix Bouvier, Bilan du débat relatif au programme Histoire et éducation à la citoyenneté du deuxième cycle de l'ordre d'enseignement secondaire qui a eu cours au Québec en 2006-2007 (Commission de consultation sur les pratiques d'accommodement reliées aux différences culturelles, janvier 2008).
sources.content: Read (text search plus key passages). The controversy began with Antoine Robitaille's Le Devoir article of 27 April 2006. Critics said the draft programme made history 'moins conflictuelle, moins politique, et davantage plurielle'. English Canada appears only as a foil. Lysiane Gagnon (La Presse, 29 April 2006) wrote that the model was 'calqué sur ce qui se fait au Canada anglais, où le multiculturalisme est devenu une religion d'État'. Critics warned that the programme left the field to 'la fondation Historica' and its Canadian nation-building. There is no mention of Granatstein, Bliss or Who Killed.
sources.role: Shows the 2006 Quebec debate did not engage the English-Canadian debate's texts.

sources.content: Radio-Canada: unveiled at the Fondation Lionel-Groulx; claims national history is 'négligée par le milieu universitaire'; no francophone university except UQAM teaches a specific course on the Conquest or the Rebellions; recommends at least 10 Quebec/Canada history courses for secondary history teachers.
